newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. Gulf buildup grows, Kuwaitis ponder cost.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf buildup grows, Kuwaitis ponder cost.

text.p: The U.S. Cavalry was on its way to oil-rich Kuwait on Wednesday to deter what Washington sees as a threat to its Arab allies from Gulf War foe Iraq.
Kuwait said it expected the United States and possibly other Gulf Arab states to share the hefty costs of the latest American troop deployment in the country occupied by Iraq in 1990-91.
"I believe Kuwait will not bear the burden alone," Kuwaiti foreign minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah told London-based Arabic-language newspaper al-Hayat.

President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he had ordered 3,500 1st Cavalry Division troops to Kuwait "to keep Saddam Hussein in a box" following the deployment in Kuwait of eight Stealth bombers and over 20 other U.S. warplanes last week and the imminent arrival in the Gulf of the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise.
U.S. officials said several hundred of the soldiers would leave Forth Hood, Texas on Wednesday. Kuwaitis said the troops were expected to start arriving in the Gulf state on Thursday afternoon.

The United States also moved a battery of U.S. Patriot air defence missile launchers and a 100-strong operational and maintenance crew to Kuwait earlier this week from another location in the Arabian peninsula, U.S. officers said.
Patriot missiles were used as defence against Iraqi Scud missiles during the 1991 Gulf War that ended Iraq's occupation of Kuwait.

Reporters in Kuwait saw eight Patriot launchers near Camp Doha U.S. military storage facility north of Kuwait City. Witnesses said the sand-coloured, coffin-shaped launchers had been installed on Tuesday and pointed north towards Iraq.

The United States earlier this month sent two Patriot anti-missile batteries and U.S. soldiers to Saudi Arabia after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. warplanes last week in the latest military confrontation between Washington and Baghdad.
The row began late last month when Baghdad's forces intervened to help a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq -- an area closed to them since the end of the Gulf war in 1991.

Western sources said U.S. pilots had started flying the newly-arrived Stealth bombers from a Kuwait airbase on training and familiarisation missions but they were not as yet flying the high-tech warplanes over Iraq.
Many Kuwaitis welcomed the impending U.S. troop deployment and some said they would be willing to help pay for it.
"Don't yell about the money we should pay, because we are willing to sacrifice our most precious assets to strengthen our freedom," liberal lawmaker Ali al-Baghli wrote in al-Qabas.

"Why don't we create a strong link with the United States and make our relations with the American nation deeper, to the extent of a union, provided that we reserve our right of sovereignty," wrote Salah al-Sayer in al-Anba.
"America...will not try to swallow us the way Iraq tries to."
Kuwaitis pressed on with a diplomatic drive to win Arab understanding of the U.S. buildup, reminding their hosts that Iraq last week called the Stealth deployment an act of war.
Kuwait says this is a new threat that has not been retracted by a country that occupied it for seven months.

Kuwaiti envoys on Tuesday visited Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Bahrain and Qatar and on Wednesday Kuwaiti Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah took the diplomatic campaign to the United Arab Emirates.

While Egypt and Syria continue to support Kuwait's right to defend itself if attacked by Iraq, they have not endorsed the latest U.S. flap with Iraq and oppose America's September 3 and 4 cruise missile attacks against targets in southern Iraq.
"They may not win resounding expressions of support but at least they will get acquiesence," said one senior diplomat.
But other diplomats in Kuwait said that with tension between Washington and Iraq apparently dropping in recent days, it was hard to understand the need to demonstrate more U.S. muscle.
